name: Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet
description: The mid-century conception of poetry as a public moral office, held by Tennyson, Browning, Arthur Hugh Clough and Matthew Arnold and named critically by Arnold's phrase "high seriousness". Its opening act is Tennyson's Poems, chiefly Lyrical (1830), the hinge between the Romantic and the Victorian lyric, followed by The Princess (1847), In Memoriam A.H.H. (privately printed 1849, title page 1850), Maud (1855) and the Arthurian Idylls of the King from 1859. Browning answered from inside with the monologues of Dramatic Lyrics (1844) and Men and Women (1855); Arnold gave up verse for criticism after Empedocles on Aetna (1852).
historical_context: The age asked its poets what it believed: Lyell's Principles of Geology (vols. 1–3, 1830–33), the anonymous Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation (1844) and the Tractarian controversy opened the questions, and the factory town and the Crimean War supplied the subjects. Public mourning attached verse to state occasions, and Tennyson's installation as poet laureate in 1850 made the poet an official functionary; "The Charge of the Light Brigade" (1854) is the mode's most quoted public poem.
aesthetic_principles: Poetry as a criticism of life; the high subject and the severe diction; moral seriousness joined to finished execution; the poet as the voice of an age to itself; art as solace and as discipline, never as licence.
defining_characteristics: The short lyric of perfected music; the long meditative or narrative poem in blank verse; the dramatic monologue as ethical probe; the medieval or classical retelling used as modern argument; the motto, the title-page epigraph and the explanatory prose paratext.
historical_significance: It fixed the Victorian canonical hierarchy — Tennyson and Browning as the age's poets, Arnold as its judge — and set the terms on which aesthetic, decadent and modernist writers later defined themselves against it.

name: Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement
description: The religious prose made by and against the Oxford Movement: the Tracts for the Times (1833–41), the sermons and pamphlet controversies of Newman, Pusey and Keble, and the long Victorian argument over authority, ritual and conscience which their prose opened. Newman's Tract 90 (1845) drove him to Rome and produced two decades later the Apologia Pro Vita Sua (1864), the period's most quoted religious autobiography; his earlier novels Loss and Gain (1848) and Callista belong to the same traffic between doctrine and narrative.
historical_context: The movement is conventionally dated from Keble's assize sermon "National Apostasy" (4 July 1833); behind it lie the government's retrenchment of the Irish Church and the church-rate agitation, before it Keble's hymn volume of 1827. Its consequences run through the ecclesiastical troubles of the later 1840s, the Gorham judgment (1850), the Essays and Reviews controversy and the Privy Council decision of 1864, and the ritualist prosecutions of the 1870s.
aesthetic_principles: The via media; reserve in religious speech; the conscience as the court of appeal; patristic and catholic authority; the Church as a visible body with a claim upon literature and upon the reader's feelings.
defining_characteristics: The tract, the sermon, the controversial pamphlet and the open letter; the periodic prose of reasoning about belief; hymn and daily-office devotion; autobiography written as legal defence; the novel of religious conversion.
historical_significance: It gave Victorian prose its model of the religious argument and, through the Broad Church and ritualist controversies, much of its vocabulary of doubt and belief; Newman's prose remains the standard case of Victorian religious style.

name: Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture
description: The prophetic, coinage-hurrying prose of Thomas Carlyle and the school of "carlylism" it created: Sartor Resartus (serialised in Fraser's Magazine 1833–34, in book form 1838), The French Revolution (1837), Chartism (1839), On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (from the 1840 course of lectures), Past and Present (1843), the Occasional Discourse on the Nigger Question (1849) and the Latter-Day Pamphlets (1850). It is the movement in which the Victorian lecture and the moral jeremiad become literary forms, and through which Ruskin, Kingsley, Froude and Arnold learned their prose.
historical_context: Written for the Edinburgh and London magazines and delivered to mechanics' institutes and to paid audiences in London and Edinburgh, it answers the Chartist platform, the Irish question and the commercial depression of the late 1840s. James Froude carries the school on: the Short Studies on Great Subjects from 1868 and the Life of Carlyle (1882); Mill's Autobiography (published 1873) is the great rival answer to it.
aesthetic_principles: Literature as moral force; the "everlasting Yea" against the "everlasting No"; the gospel of work; history written as dramatic present; hero-worship as the substance of history; contempt for the "cash nexus" and for parliamentary talk.
defining_characteristics: The coined compound, the apostrophe, the exclamation and the broken periodic sentence; the lecture and the pamphlet; the jeremiad on "captains of industry"; the quarrel with laissez-faire; the apostrophised dead hero.
historical_significance: It supplied the Victorian language of hero-worship, of the "condition-of-England question" and of industrial duty, and made the prophetic prose lecture a permanent literary institution on both sides of the Atlantic.

name: Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel
description: The fiction of the 1840s and 1850s written out of the "two nations" panic and the Chartist agitations, which made wage labour, the lock-out, the hand-loom weaver and the starving town subjects of serious prose fiction: Gaskell's Mary Barton: A Tale of Manchester Life (1848) and North and South (serialised 1854–55, in books 1855), Disraeli's Coningsby (1844) and Sybil, or The Two Nations (1845), Kingsley's Yeast (1848) and Alton Locke (1850), and Dickens's Hard Times (serialised 1854) as the mode's late satiric reckoning.
historical_context: Carlyle's phrase names the problem these novels answer. Their occasions are the distress and the "Plug Plot" of 1842, the Chartist petition of 1848, the cholera years, the ten-hours and factory legislation, and the Christian-socialist and cooperative agitation carried in London by Kingsley and F. D. Maurice; Gaskell writes from Manchester Unitarian circles, Disraeli from Young England.
aesthetic_principles: Fiction as social evidence; sympathy compelled across class lines; the indictment of the wage relation; the industrial sermon addressed to the reader rather than to a party.
defining_characteristics: The mill town and the tenement; the strike, the lock-out and the riot; the dying child and the consumption of the operative; the Irish navvy in the English city; the reconciliation plot that marries capital to labour.
historical_significance: It created the industrial novel as a permanent branch of English fiction and forced the language of class, wage and factory into the mid-century mainstream.

name: Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot
description: The popular realism of the late 1850s and 1860s, built from stolen inheritances, bigamy, poison, asylum confinement and disguised identity, and set not in Apennine castles but in modern English houses: Collins's The Woman in White (serialised 1859–60, three volumes 1860), No Name (1862), Armadale (1866) and The Moonstone (1868); Braddon's Lady Audley's Secret (1862) and Aurora Floyd (1863); Mrs Henry Wood's East Lynne (1861).
historical_context: The mode flourished in the cheap weeklies and the library triple-decker and moved at once to the stage in the sensation drama of the 1860s and 1870s. Collins, who began as Dickens's contributor and collaborator (The Frozen Deep, 1857, and No Thoroughfare, 1867), is its technical centre, while Braddon and Wood edited the magazines that carried it; the expanding railway bookstall and circulating-library trade made its audience.
aesthetic_principles: A single "sensation" prolonged through a plot; the modern domestic world as the true scene of terror; probability produced by documentary effect; the reader's detective interest as the engine of the book.
defining_characteristics: Competing first-person witness statements; diary, letter, report, will and medico-legal paper inserted as evidence; the woman whose reputation or property is the plot's stake; the private asylum, the train, the lime-light and the laudanum cup.
historical_significance: Sensation fiction created the modern plot-driven bestseller, professionalised women's popular authorship, and supplied the narrative machinery from which the detective story was separated.

name: Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature
description: The programme of the Germ circle (1848–50) — Dante Gabriel Rossetti, William Holman Hunt and John Everett Millais, with Coventry Patmore, and at one remove William Morris, Edward Burne-Jones and Christina Rossetti — which demanded "complete sincerity and thorough study of Nature" and made the poem a picture. Its literary course runs from Rossetti's early Botticelli tale Hand and Soul (written 1849–50, printed in the early 1860s) through Morris's The Defence of Guenevere (1858) and The Earthly Paradise (1868–70) to Rossetti's Poems (1870) and the sonnet-and-picture body of The House of Life (published 1881).
historical_context: Ruskin's defence of the brotherhood after the controversy over Millais's domestic Christ in the House of His Parents gave the movement its patron and its doctrine; the single monthly issues of The Germ (1850) mark its formal beginning; the decorative firm founded in 1861 and the later Kelmscott Press carry it into the making of books. Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) belongs to the same circle and partly repudiates it.
aesthetic_principles: "Truth to Nature"; serious subjects treated with literal fidelity and dense detail; colour and the concrete image preferred to generalisation; the poem and the picture as one object; the medieval and Arthurian as living rather than antiquarian material.
defining_characteristics: The pictorial narrative poem; the sonnet written to or on a picture and the emblazoned title-page; ballad stanza with archaising diction; the decorated and illustrated book; the insistent named woman with her hair, flowers and sleeves.
historical_significance: It fused literary and visual practice, gave Victorian poetry its intense imagistic diction, and through Morris and Pater leads directly into aestheticism and the arts-and-crafts book.

name: Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art
description: Ruskin's prose campaign which read painting, architecture and wages as one moral system: Modern Painters (vol. I, 1843), The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849), The Stones of Venice (1851–53, with its chapter "The Nature of Gothic"), Sesame and Lilies (1860), Unto This Last (serialised in the Cornhill Magazine, 1860) and The Storm-Cloud of the Nineteenth Century (1884).
historical_context: The Great Exhibition of 1851 and its language of improvement, the Gothic Revival churches and offices built after Pugin published Contrasts in 1841, the Lancashire and Sheffield wage conflicts, and Ruskin's Oxford professorship held from 1870 give the writing its occasions; the Whistler libel action and verdict of 1877–78 are its public crisis.
aesthetic_principles: The "life" and the "law" of a material; no great art without a great society; the moral value of ornament and of the workman's pleasure in his work; wealth defined as the maintenance of lives rather than as accumulation; accurate sight as a duty.
defining_characteristics: The long descriptive paragraph that turns observation into argument; the architectural and typological reading of a surface; the lecture, the household manual and the open letter on wages; the tract against political economy.
historical_significance: It made art criticism a social science, created the ethical case against industrial capitalism that William Morris inherited, and formed the period's standard prose of description from Turner to the Venice lagune.

name: Arnold and the Criticism of Culture
description: Matthew Arnold's programme of criticism and the school it founded: the Essays in Criticism of 1865 and their second series of 1888, which contains "The Study of Poetry" and its touchstone test, with Culture and Anarchy (1869), Literature and Dogma (1873) and Discourses in America (1885). His earlier verse is the poetic arm of the same position: "Sohrab and Rustum" and "The Scholar-Gipsy" (1853), "Stanzas from the Grande Chartreuse" (published 1855) and "Thyrsis" (1866).
historical_context: It is written for the reading public made by the elementary codes, the school boards and the university reforms of the 1870s; Arnold speaks as a schools inspector and as the poet who turned to criticism. Its rivals are Froude's and Carlyle's prophetic prose and, at the century's close, Pater's hedonist critique.
aesthetic_principles: Criticism as a disinterested pursuit of "the best that has been known and thought"; culture as the study of perfection and not as aesthetic materialism or as machinery; the touchstone and "high seriousness"; the authority of style and diction.
defining_characteristics: The critical essay of ideas addressed to a general public; the lecture; the controversial prose against "Philistines" and the "Populace"; the ironised personification of national types; the phrase made technical vocabulary.
historical_significance: It established the idea of "culture" and the modern discipline of literary criticism, and left the terms — "high seriousness", "touchstone", "Hebraism and Hellenism", "sweetness and light" — through which English literature is still taught.

name: Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire
description: The masculine, Christian and athletic programme of the late 1840s and 1850s associated with Thomas Hughes, Charles Kingsley and F. D. Maurice's Working Men's College (founded 1854), and the boys' fiction it produced: Hughes's Tom Brown's School Days (1857) and Tom Brown at Oxford (1861), Kingsley's Westward Ho! (1855) and Ballantyne's The Coral Island (1858). Its late-century descendants are the boys' empire story — Haggard's King Solomon's Mines (1885) — and Kipling's Kim (1901), the last book inside the period's boundary.
historical_context: Public-school reform and the Clarendon enquiries, the "muscular" answer to over-civilisation and to the cholera town, the Volunteer Force raised in the invasion scare of 1859–60, the emigration societies and the mission field form its social setting; the Christian Social Union and the social gospel of the 1880s carry its religious argument forward.
aesthetic_principles: The trained body in the service of God and country; courage, fairness and the fourth-form code as moral categories; character built by games, fagging and rough-rider discipline; the Anglo-Saxon as a historical instrument.
defining_characteristics: The school story with its bully and its cricket match; the island or frontier tale in which boys govern themselves; the seafaring romance of English destiny; the cadet and the games story; the muscular sermon addressed to the young man.
historical_significance: It created the British school story and the boys' imperial romance, two of the century's most durable popular forms, and supplied the still-familiar moral language of "muscular Christianity".

name: The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice
description: The Victorian perfection of the poem in which a speaker unwittingly reveals a character not the poet's own, and its extension into the dramatic lyric. Its landmarks are Browning's Pippa Passes (1841), Dramatic Lyrics (1844), Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845) and the collected Dramatic Works (from 1868), Men and Women (1855) and The Ring and the Book (1868–69), with Clough's ironic narratives and meditations of the 1850s and Arnold's masked interlocutors.
historical_context: This is a poetry for readers rather than for audiences: the annual, the two-volume collected edition and the review are its publication world. Elizabeth Barrett Browning belongs to the same culture of the constructed speaking self, with Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850) and the verse-novel Aurora Leigh (1856).
aesthetic_principles: The masked speaker and the half-undisclosed listener; involuntary self-revelation as the means of ethical judgment; the refusal of the confident first person; character built out of diction, syntax and the wrong word chosen.
defining_characteristics: A single utterance before a silent auditor; the historical or literary "case"; parenthetical self-correction and the quoted other; irony achieved without commentary; the lyric whose speaker is explicitly not the poet.
historical_significance: It is the Victorian gift to modern poetry: the technique of the constructed speaker, transmitted through Swinburne and Hardy to the twentieth century, and its critical vocabulary is still ours.

name: Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade
description: The doctrine of the autonomous artefact, "art for art's sake", as it took institutional shape in Britain from the mid-1860s to the 1890s: Swinburne's Poems and Ballads (1866); Pater's Renaissance studies of 1873 with their famous conclusion, then Marius the Epicurean (1885), Imaginary Portraits (1887) and Appreciation (1889); Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray (in Lippincott's Magazine 1890, with the prefatory manifesto in the book of 1891), his comedies of the early 1890s and The Ballad of Reading Gaol (1898); and the little magazines from The Yellow Book (1894–97) to The Savoy (1896). Arthur Symons's The Symbolist Movement in Literature (1899) gives it a criticism.
historical_context: The Oxford and London aesthetic debate of the 1870s, artistic dress and the decorated house, the Whistler trial, and the parody of the movement on the comic stage all precede it; the trials of 1895 and the reaction after them end it. Wilde's De Profundis, written in prison and published after 1901, falls outside the window.
aesthetic_principles: Art for art's sake; style as the moral act of prose; "the hard, gemlike flame"; the critic's impression and the paradox; the independence of form from doctrine; the refinement of sensation as an end.
defining_characteristics: The little magazine and the decorated book; the essay of the paradox and the dialogue on art; the prose poem and the decadent verse of refrain and echo; the society comedy that argues by wit; the illustrated cover and the black-bordered yellow book.
historical_significance: It separated the modern idea of literary art from civic and moral instruction, created the small press and the coterie magazine, and made the stylish critic a public role.

name: The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel
description: The late-Victorian fiction and polemic which turned the "woman question" into a plot and a market: Schreiner's The Story of an African Farm (1883), Meredith's Diana of the Crossways (1885), Gissing's New Grub Street (1891) and The Odd Women (1893), the "marriage strike" and free-love controversy of the mid-1890s, Grant Allen's The Woman Who Did (1895), and the marriage-market and fallen-man fiction of Thomas Hardy, George Moore and Murray.
historical_context: Its conditions are the Married Women's Property Act (1882), the repeal campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts and the protest mobilisation of 1885–86, the college and medical-school openings for women, the divorce court and its published cases, and the feminist journalism of the 1890s; Ibsen's problem drama reaches the English stage and the English novel in translations and adaptations during the 1890s.
aesthetic_principles: Fiction as a laboratory of conduct and a piece of evidence; the marriage plot deliberately broken open; the argumentative novel whose thesis its own characters state; plain statement of the facts of sex against the older reticence.
defining_characteristics: The railway, the typewriter, the college and the furnished lodging; the educated wage-earning heroine; the free-love quarrel and the "new man"; the novel which answers another novel; the problem play as its stage equivalent.
historical_significance: It forced marriage law, work, the double standard and the biology of sex into English fiction as topics of public argument, and created the "New Woman" debate that ran into the Edwardian suffrage movement. ### 2B. AMERICAN MOVEMENTS (9)

name: Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum
description: The revolt inside American Unitarianism, centred on Concord and Boston and conducted in the lecture hall: Emerson's Nature (1836), the address "The American Scholar" (delivered 1837), "Self-Reliance" and "The Over-Soul" in Essays: Second Series (1844), Thoreau's Walden (1854) and his essay on civil disobedience (published 1849), and the pages of The Dial (1840–44), edited successively by Margaret Fuller and by Ripley. Bronson Alcott's school and community experiments, and the fiction of his daughters in the 1860s and 1870s, belong to its orbit.
historical_context: The Unitarian controversy over the miracles and the nature of God, the lyceum and lecture circuit that carried the new prose to Western and New England towns, the Transcendental club formed in 1836, Brook Farm and the Fourierist communities of the late 1840s, and the anti-slavery platform on which Parker and Phillips Garrison spoke, are its occasions; Carlyle and German Idealism reach it through the Edinburgh Review and the Dial.
aesthetic_principles: Intuition and the "Over-Soul" above miracle and institution; the infinite in every human breast; self-reliance and the unwritten law; nature as a system of symbols; the American mind released from European book-learning.
defining_characteristics: The prose lecture, the address and the aphoristic essay; the journal of deliberate observation; the manifesto of intellectual independence; the tract for the reform society; the idealist theory of language.
historical_significance: It created the first home-grown American intellectual idiom, made the lecture a national literary form, and set the terms — self-reliance, nonconformity, the scholar's obligation — on which later American prose argued.

name: Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance
description: Hawthorne and Melville, the American romance that inherits and interrogates New England Calvinism. Hawthorne's course runs from Twice-Told Tales (1837) and Mosses from an Old Manse (1846) through The Scarlet Letter (1850), The House of the Seven Gables (1851), The Blithedale Romance (1852) to The Marble Faun (1860); Melville's from Typee (1846) and White-Jacket (1850) through Moby-Dick (1851), Pierre (1852), the "Encantadas" pieces and Benito Cereno (in Putnam's 1855–56), The Piazza Tales (1856) and The Confidence-Man (1857).
historical_context: The decay of the Calvinist theology that still governed American moral vocabulary, the custom-house and surveyorships that gave both writers an income, the reform and communal experiments of the 1840s, the fugitive-slave crisis that produced Benito Cereno, and the publishing difficulties of the American London trade.
aesthetic_principles: The Romance, claiming a "truth of the human heart" above photographic realism; the allegorical situation retained inside modern prose; suspicion of benevolent systems and of the reformer's optimism; the mutable interpretation and the sceptical question.
defining_characteristics: The moral hieroglyphic and the emblazoned tapestry; the meditative, unreliable or interrogating narrator; the ship, the custom house and the old manse as framing spaces; the secret sin and the public pillory; the philosophical whale.
historical_significance: It supplied the central nineteenth-century American canon, and its self-conscious theory of the Romance is the source of the American distinction between romance and realism.

name: The Second American Renaissance and the Whitman-Dickinson Lyric
description: The lyric revolution that made American verse modern: Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855, reissued and enlarged through the edition he was preparing when he died in 1891), the war sequences of Drum-Taps (1865) and the Lincoln elegies, and the poems of Emily Dickinson — more than a thousand composed in the 1860s, first published in a book only in 1890, with a second series in 1891 and her Letters in 1894.
historical_context: Its occasion is the national crisis: the first edition of 1855, the war years when Dickinson wrote most fast, and the post-bellum consolidation of a national canon in which the recital circuit, the magazine and the school and family anthology fixed the public poets.
aesthetic_principles: The free line, the catalog and the long breath as a democratic form; the compressed stanza, the internal rhyme and slant as an interior form; poetry as the adequate speech of an age and a continent; the body and the soul without hierarchy.
defining_characteristics: The long improvisation and the anaphoric roll; the hymn-metre poem turned against itself; the war lyric and the funeral elegy; the titleless poem known by its first line; the editorial controversy over the uncertain text.
historical_significance: It is the founding event of modern American poetry, and its two opposed lines — Whitman's expansive free line and Dickinson's contracted ballad stanza — remain the available American choices.

name: Mark Twain and the Vernacular Performance
description: The making of a written American voice out of spoken American performance: the "jumping frog" tale first published in 1865, Innocents Abroad (1869), Roughing It (1872), The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Life on the Mississippi (1883), Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (published 1884 in Boston and 1885 in Hartford) and the race-and-law tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894).
historical_context: The Mississippi pilot's and cub's craft, the Virginia City and Comstock silver booms, the special correspondent's trip, the Hartford household and the failure of his own publishing house, and the financial crash of 1894: all conditions of a literature made out of reporting, lecturing and story-telling to a live audience.
aesthetic_principles: Talk as the medium of prose; the local dialect recorded and graded; the tall-tale breath, the joke and the "stretch"; the vernacular eye turned on the civilized forms — the Romance, the travel-book, the boy's story.
defining_characteristics: The first-person yarn with its frame of hearth and platform; the mock-travel book; the boy's adventure; the dialect sketch of race and frontier justice; the burlesque quotation from the older Romances.
historical_significance: It established the American vernacular as a literary medium, and the post-1884 Huck remains the reference point for every claim about an authentic American style.

name: American Realism and the Howells Program
description: The post-bellum school that demanded of fiction "the essentials of veracity", and its theory: Howells's Venetian Life (1866), A Modern Instance (1882), The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885), A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890), The Landlord at Lion's Head (1897) and Criticism and Fiction (1891), alongside Henry James's American fictions — The American (1877), Daisy Miller (1878–79), The Portrait of a Lady (1881) and, at the century's close, The Turn of the Screw (1898).
historical_context: The post-war marriage of New York and Boston publishing, The Atlantic Monthly (from 1857) and the great monthlies as its organ, the rise of the professional editor and of the metropolitan novel of manners, and the transatlantic circulation that made the two literatures one field.
aesthetic_principles: The homely and unlovely realities of common American life made a fit subject for art; the refusal of the sensational plot; the moral seriousness of the drawing-room, the office and the board of direction; a large, free and generous dealing with things as they are.
defining_characteristics: The domestic and business novel of ordinary experience; the tale of the invisible power of money and manners; the international theme of American innocence before Europe; the editor-critic as a literary figure.
historical_significance: It supplied the period's own name for its mature fiction — "realism" — and the label, with all its later disputes, still organises the account of American literature after the Civil War.

name: Local Colour and the Regionalist School
description: The writing of American "sections" as scenery, speech and type: the California stories Bret Harte published in The Overland Monthly from 1868, the Vermont and New Hampshire narratives of the 1870s–1880s, the New England village tales of Mary E. Freeman and of Mary Wilkins Freeman, the Maine coastal tales of Sarah Orne Jewett — gathered in The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896) — the Georgia black-country tales of Joel Chandler Harris, and the Louisiana Acadian and Creole fiction of George Washington Cable and of Kate Chopin.
historical_context: It is a post-Reconstruction literature of reunion, in which sections are marketed as picturesque differences: the illustrated monthly, the regional lecture tour, the railroad and the summer colony, the "sectional" typology of the 1880s, and the South's literary department.
aesthetic_principles: The group of types and the speech of a place as the true subject; the "local colour" of dress, dialect and topography preferred to plot; the sketch rather than the plotted intrigue.
defining_characteristics: The short descriptive tale; dialect spelling and the oral frame; the characteristic "group" of a coastal village, a mining camp or a river settlement; the retold folktale; the sentimental-ironic treatment of the disappearing type.
historical_significance: It established the American short story as a regional form and made dialect, and then the "section", the technical ground of American fiction from Harris to the 1920s.

name: American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy
description: The American naturalist school of the 1890s, which read character as the product of heredity, environment and money: Crane's Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893) and The Red Badge of Courage (serialised 1894, in books 1895); Norris's McTeague (1899), with Vandover privately printed in the mid-1890s; Chopin's The Awakening (1899); and Paul Laurence Dunbar's poems and prose of the 1890s.
historical_context: The doctrine is an Americaned Darwin and Spencer; its social scene is the great city, the strike and the depressed labour market of the 1890s; its publication venue is the mass monthly, the ten-cent edition, the little magazine and the New York and Chicago Bohemia.
aesthetic_principles: Man read as a function of heredity, environment and the passions; the case history and the clinical eye; the refusal of the reward plot; the brute within.
defining_characteristics: The case-study novel; the crowd, the machine and the mine; the instinctual body and its defeat; the compressed war and city tale; the frank treatment of sex, labour and the colour line.
historical_significance: It is the first American school to define itself in a doctrine of method, and it carried American fiction into the twentieth century.

name: South-Western Humour and the Tall-Tale Sketch
description: The comic literature of the southern and western frontier, in which the boast exceeds the fact: the sporting and political sketches of the South-Western frontier newspapers and almanacs of the 1830s and 1840s — the school later critics named the "backwoods humorists" — and the California comic tale of the 1850s to the 1870s, in which Harte and Twain both begin.
historical_context: Its venues are the frontier weekly and the almanac, the Mississippi steamboat and the mining camp, the political stump and the platform; its audience was rural and popular, and it is the first American literature to sell in bulk to its own lower-middle and western readers.
aesthetic_principles: The elaborate, matter-of-fact lie; the one-upmanship of the boast and of the yarn told in high good humour; the laughing, self-congratulating community.
defining_characteristics: The tall tale, the trick story and the comic debate; the dialect of the sporting paper; the frame of the bar-room, camp-fire and stump; the tall, lying hero with his horse and his rifle.
historical_significance: It was the first native American vernacular style, and the technical ancestor of the sketch, the frame narrative and the tall voice of Twain.

name: The Aesthetic Turn in 1890s America
description: "Art for art's sake" in the United States: the "artistic" verse and criticism of the late 1870s and 1880s, including Edmund Clarence Stedman's critical volumes and anthologies; the American little magazines of the 1890s, of which The Chap-Book, started in Chicago in 1894, is the most visible; the aesthetic and decadent short story and the novel of the artist; and the decorative book and the illustrated cover, carried across from London by contributors to The Yellow Book.
historical_context: The American aesthetic movement arrives with the decorative and interior-design vogue of the Gilded Age, with the Boston and New York "art" world, and with the magazine and the little press; and it is overlaid, and overwhelmed, by the realist, regionalist and naturalist debates.
aesthetic_principles: The autonomy of the art object; beauty against instruction; the "artistic" personality; the magazine and the decorated cover as the site of taste.
defining_characteristics: The little magazine; the aesthetic lyric; the novel of the artist; the "artistic" interior and its furniture; the critical anthology and its categories.
historical_significance: It created the American little magazine and prepared the American lyric anthology and the repertoires of the 1910s and 1920s.
